# Research notes on Job 15 (Eliphaz's second speech)

**Coverage:** Most of these notes come from Enduring Word (Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott, Gill, Matthew Henry, Clarke, Barnes, Constable, JFB, Coffman, the NET notes and Bible Hub's study notes. I couldn't find any page on the allowed sites for vv. 3 and 33, or any bibleodyssey.org page on this chapter. Some Pulpit Commentary notes (vv. 4, 7–8, 11–12, 19–23) come from a page I read in full, so they have no citation tags. Their URL is https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm.

## Overview
- Eliphaz is harsher and cruder here than in his first speech (ch. 4). Most of the chapter describes how the wicked suffer, and it rests on cause-and-effect theology: if Job suffers, he must secretly be a hypocrite. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/
- Ellicott: Eliphaz repeats the familiar teaching that the wicked are punished in this life. That rule breaks down completely in a case like Job's, unless Job really is one of the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-15.html
- Matthew Henry: Eliphaz believes the wicked are always miserable. From that he wrongly concludes that the miserable are always wicked, so Job must be. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_015.cfm

## Verse by verse

**v. 1:** Benson: Eliphaz is annoyed. He charges Job with conceit about his own knowledge, with arrogance for brushing aside the older men's experience, and with irreverence for challenging God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/15-1.htm

**v. 2:** "Empty counsel" literally means "knowledge of wind": vain and without substance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm
- Guzik, quoting Andersen: "belly" is the literal word. The verb may even mean "empty," so Eliphaz is crudely calling Job's speeches belly wind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/
- Constable: the east wind was the dreaded desert sirocco. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-15.html
- Gill: Job did not actually say anything empty enough to deserve comparison with wind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/15-2.html

**v. 4:** Pulpit: Job's bold appeals (ch. 13) made Eliphaz think he had abandoned reverence. Yet Job keeps showing a strong sense of God's purity, which should have spared him this charge. "Meditation" is the better reading. Eliphaz's point is that Job's words upset devout people and so spread irreligion.
- JFB: Eliphaz reasons that if Job were right, and God ignores the righteous in their suffering while the wicked prosper, all devotion would come to an end. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_015.cfm
- Guzik: Eliphaz is simply wrong. Chapter 1 shows Job was a man of prayer. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/job-15/

**v. 5:** Ellicott: the Hebrew can mean "your mouth teaches your iniquity" or "your iniquity teaches your mouth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-15.html
- Pulpit: "crafty" is the word used of the serpent in Genesis 3:1. Eliphaz is accusing Job of dressing up real impiety as religion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm
- Gill (tagged Baptist/Calvinist): the wickedness in Job's heart made his mouth speak (Matthew 12:34). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/15-5.html

**v. 6:** Pulpit compares the scene to Jesus' accusers: "what further need of witnesses?" (Matthew 26:65–66). It notes that malice loves to misread what righteous people say. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm

**v. 7:** Pulpit: this is a scoff, not a real question. Is Job claiming the flawless mind of the first man, or to be older than the hills?
- Guzik: God later uses a similar argument (chs. 38–39). The difference is that Eliphaz "knows" Job is a sinner, while God knows Job doesn't understand creation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/

**v. 8:** Pulpit: no human being sits in God's secret council (compare Jeremiah 23:18 and Romans 11:34). Eliphaz turns Job's own jibe from 12:2 back on him.
- Bible Hub's study notes: the "council of God" is the heavenly assembly (1 Kings 22:19). https://biblehub.com/job/15.htm

**v. 9:** Pulpit: Job may not have known more facts, but he had sharper spiritual insight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm
- Andersen, via Guzik: Job only claimed to be as intelligent as his friends (12:3), not to have all the wisdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/

**v. 10:** Pulpit: "with us" means "on our side," with all the greybeards past and present. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm
- Clarke disagrees. He thinks Eliphaz means himself and his two friends, and he cites a Targum that names them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-15.html

**v. 11:** Pulpit: the "consolations of God" are the friends' promises that Job would be restored if he repented. Guzik: Eliphaz treated his own advice as God's comfort, so rejecting it meant rejecting God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/job/job-15.cfm
- Pulpit Homiletics: in fact the friends were not bringing God's consolations. Their doctrine of exact, immediate payback is not true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/job/15.htm

**v. 12:** Pulpit: the verb behind "flash" appears only here, and its meaning is very uncertain.

**v. 13:** Constable: Eliphaz took Job's frustrated prayers as rebellion, which they were not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/15-15.html
- Pulpit: neither Eliphaz nor his friends ever name which of Job's words were impious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm

**v. 14:** Pulpit: this is beside the point. The real question was not whether Job was sinless, but whether he had sinned badly enough to deserve this suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm
- JFB: Eliphaz uses Job's own phrase "born of woman" (14:1) against him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_015.cfm
- Constable: Eliphaz was right that everyone is a corrupt sinner, but wrong about why Job suffered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-15.html

**v. 15:** Pulpit: the "holy ones" are angels. It calls Eliphaz's view of their untrustworthiness peculiar and not supported by the rest of Scripture. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/15.htm
- Clarke (Wesleyan): only God cannot change. Saints and angels can fall, because their goodness comes from God and depends on him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-15.html

**v. 16:** NET note: man commits evil as easily, and in as large amounts, as he drinks water. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Job&chapter=15&verse=16
- Pulpit: the target is clearly Job, not people in general. Cambridge, also on Bible Hub, says "man" means mankind in general, though the words clearly hint at Job. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/15-16.htm
- Poole: true as a general statement, but wrongly applied to Job. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/15-16.htm

**vv. 17–18:** Clarke: Eliphaz quotes old wise sayings that are good in themselves but wrongly applied to Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-15.html
- Constable: Eliphaz relies on experience, Bildad on tradition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/8-16.html
- Pulpit: the "wise men" may have been Eastern sages, or Egyptians or Babylonians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/15-18.htm

**v. 19:** Pulpit: this looks back to an early time when peoples lived undisturbed, so the teaching was handed down pure.
- Henry: Eliphaz is answering Job's claim that the earth is given to the wicked (9:24), and he takes a swipe at the Sabean and Chaldean raids on Job. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_015.cfm

**v. 20:** Pulpit calls this an overstatement and points to Psalm 73:3–5.
- Guzik's paraphrase of Eliphaz: only the wicked suffer like you, so you must be wicked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/
- Constable: the section begins and ends with images of childbirth (vv. 20, 35). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-15.html

**v. 21:** Coffman: the line about destruction coming "in his prosperity" is aimed straight at Job's story. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-15.html
- Pulpit: "the destroyer" could be the destroying angel, an avenger of blood, or a raider.

**v. 22:** Pulpit compares Cain's fear in Genesis 4:14.

**v. 23:** Pulpit reads "wanders for bread." The BSB's "food for vultures" follows the Septuagint but needs a small change to the Hebrew vowels.
- Ellicott thinks the picture is overdrawn here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-15.html

**v. 24:** Pulpit: a veiled reference to the disasters that crushed Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-15.html

**vv. 25–26:** Pulpit: the image is a charging bull with neck lowered, then a warrior with a heavy studded shield. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-15.html
- Guzik: by implication Eliphaz is accusing Job of attacking God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/

**v. 27:** Smick, via Guzik: fat was a sign of wealth, so Eliphaz is admitting the wicked do prosper, but only for a while. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/

**v. 28:** Ellicott: this finishes the portrait of the proud tyrant living in cities that will become ruins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-15.html

**v. 29:** Clarke: Eliphaz is indirectly calling Job a tyrant and oppressor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-15.html
- Ellicott: the word behind "possessions" occurs only here, so its meaning is uncertain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/job-15.html

**v. 30:** JFB: the "shoots" are his children (compare 1:18–19), and the "breath" is God's anger. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_015.cfm
- Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary: a false prediction, overturned by Job 42:10–17. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/job-15.html

**v. 31:** Pulpit Homiletics: the self-deceived man is Job. That isn't true of Job, but it is true of many, so we should examine our own assurance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-15.html

**v. 32:** The "branch" line echoes the fallen tyrant of Isaiah 14:19. https://biblehub.com/job/15.htm
- Coffman: the implied prophecies of early death never came true. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-15.html

**v. 34:** JFB: Eliphaz hints that the "fire of God" (1:16) fell because Job took bribes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Job/Job_015.cfm

**v. 35:** Pulpit: the Hebrews often spoke of the inner organs as the seat of thought. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-15.html
- Andersen, quoted by Constable: Eliphaz called Job a windbag but ends his own speech with a pile of words. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-15.html
- Guzik: in this indirect way Eliphaz accuses Job of hypocrisy, bribery, stirring up trouble and lying. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-15/

## Where Protestant traditions differ
The writers I read don't really disagree. Calvinist Gill, Wesleyan Clarke, Henry and Guzik all say Eliphaz's general truths are wrongly applied to Job.

The one doctrinal theme is vv. 14–16 and human sinfulness:
- **Reformed/Baptist:** Gill says man is "naturally and originally filthy" from conception, and only Christ's blood can make him clean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/15-16.htm
- **Wesleyan/Methodist:** Clarke stresses that a bad man thirsts after sin, while a good man thirsts after righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/dby/job/15-16.html
- **Benson** (also Methodist): the friends clearly believed in original sin and total depravity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/15-1.htm

I found nothing from Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican sources on this chapter.

## Other views
- **Modern scholarship (NET):** see the note on v. 16. I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org.
- **Catholic:** Haydock on v. 31 notes that the Hebrew and Greek read "vanity shall be his reward." Quoting Menochius, he adds that the man could still be safe if he repented. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/15-31.html
- **Orthodox and popular modern teaching:** I found nothing from Orthodox sources, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
